title: 11.2 PART I STRATEGY LAB
what_this_is: **Eleven real questions off your own 11.2 Part I test.** The right answer is already shown on every one, with the proof highlighted in the passage. Your job is to see how the proof gets you there.
**These are items the class struggled with or that are worth a second look together.** It is not the whole test, and it is not new material. You have already seen every one.
Two of the eleven (Q14 and Q25) have no passage. Those are recall items, and the page says so.

types.lead: Every Part I question is one of six moves you already know. Each question below names its move in the same language as your packets and the wall: **the Frame position, the move, and the skill line it feeds.**

how_to_work.head: HOW TO READ EACH QUESTION
how_to_work.lead: *Same four questions you ask of every document, all year: Q1 Sourcing, Q2 Claim & Evidence, Q3 Perspective Check, Q4 Civic Connection. Each question below names the one it tests. Here is the order to read it in.*
steps: **Read the question first, not the passage.** Know what you're looking for.
**Q1 SOURCING.** Start at the source line: the date, the author, and what kind of document it is. Free information, before you read a word of the passage.
**Q2 CLAIM & EVIDENCE.** Read the whole passage, highlights included. What is this document arguing or showing? That's the claim. The four answer choices are what you're testing it against.

**The right answer is already shown, and the highlighted words are why.** Whatever the question really tests (Perspective Check, Civic Connection, whichever the page names), the proof is in those few words.
**Read Why it's right, then Watch for, then go on to the next one.**

notes.head: CONTENT NOTE — THE MARSHALL COURT AND THE ELASTIC CLAUSE
body: SIX OF THE ELEVEN RUN ON THE SAME FIGHT

Marbury v. Madison (1803, Q10), the Antifederalist warnings about the “elastic clause” during ratification (Q11, Q18, Q26), and McCulloch v. Maryland (1819, Q14 and Q15) are not six separate topics — they are one argument that runs across thirty years.

**The Constitution gives Congress power to make laws “necessary and proper” for carrying out its other powers (Article I, Section 8) — the elastic clause.** Antifederalists in 1787-88 warned this clause had no real limit and would let Congress take on power the Constitution never listed. Nobody settled who was right until John Marshall's Court did, case by case: Marbury (1803) first established that the Court itself gets to say what the Constitution means; McCulloch (1819) then used that power to rule that the elastic clause DOES reach new cases Congress never listed by name (chartering a national bank), and that federal law wins when it conflicts with a state's — **federal supremacy.**

**Q15 is the federalism item on this test — its answer is the word “supremacy” itself.** Read Q10, 11, 14, 15, 18 and 26 as one continuous argument, not six unrelated questions, and the whole test gets easier.

notes.head: CONTENT NOTE — THE McCULLOCH PAIR
body: Q14 and Q15 are the same case, back-to-back on the Jan. 2025 exam — Q5 and Q6. Read them as one case doing two jobs: Q14 asks what the ruling settled; Q15 asks what PRINCIPLE it's an example of. Same case, two different six-move questions.

body: NOTHING HERE IS SCORED, AND NOTHING IS KEPT
Eleven questions, each one coached from the passage to the answer. **If you can say why each right answer is right, you are done.**

items.watch: Two choices describe a power no branch has ever actually had (a lower court reversing the Supreme Court; the judiciary alone amending the Constitution) — rule those out on structure before you even get to the history.
items.stem: What is one important consequence of the Supreme Court’s decision in Marbury v. Madison?

options.1: The Supreme Court’s decisions may be reversed by a lower court.
options.2: Amending the Constitution became the sole responsibility of the judicial branch.
options.3: The power of the judicial branch was expanded.
options.4: Nominations of Supreme Court Justices had to be approved by a majority vote of Congress.

passage.text:
The Constitution is either the highest law, which ordinary laws cannot change, or it is just another ordinary law, and Congress can change it whenever it pleases. …

“It is emphatically the province and duty of the judicial department to say what the law is.” (It is the courts' job to say what the law means.) …

“A law repugnant to the constitution is void” (a law that conflicts with the Constitution is not a real law; it has no force).
passage.citation: Source: Marbury v. Madison, 1803, Chief Justice John Marshall, for the Supreme Court (adapted)
passage._from: DOC_BANK unit02C-marbury-1803-adapted.json - named by item 0824-mc10's own stimulus_refs

spans: duty of the judicial department to say what the law is
A law repugnant to the constitution is void
items.why: Chief Justice Marshall writes that it is the “duty of the judicial department to say what the law is” and that “A law repugnant to the constitution is void.” If the Court can throw out a law because it conflicts with the Constitution, the judicial branch has gained power over the laws Congress passes. That is the power of the judicial branch expanded: choice 3.

items.watch: Due process and equal protection are real constitutional terms, but they protect individuals FROM government power — they are not grants of power TO Congress, which is what a worried Antifederalist in 1788 is writing about.
items.stem: Which provision in the Constitution is the author of this passage questioning?

passage.text: . . . My object is to consider that undefined, unbounded and immense power which is comprised [included] in the following clause—“And to make all laws which shall be necessary and proper for carrying into execution the foregoing powers, and all other powers vested by this constitution in the government of the United States; or in any department or offices thereof.” Under such a clause as this, can anything be said to be reserved and kept back from Congress? . . .
passage._from: live stimulus-11-2.json item 0823-mc01 - same NYSED crop unit02-0823-mc01.png, transcribed word for word

spans: And to make all laws which shall be necessary and proper
items.why: The author is worried about an “undefined, unbounded and immense power” that Congress has. He points to the clause that creates it, which says “And to make all laws which shall be necessary and proper” for carrying out Congress's other powers. A clause that lets Congress make any law it calls necessary and proper is the elastic clause, choice 3.

items.era: The New Republic · Washington & Religious Liberty (1790)
items.watch: A choice can name a real historical issue of the era and still be wrong, if THIS letter doesn't actually speak to it. Being a real 1790s topic is not the same as being what this source proves.
items.stem: This passage would be most useful to a historian studying

options.1: colonial ideas about leadership in the Americas
options.2: religious freedom in early United States history

passage.text:
To the Hebrew [Jewish] Congregation in Newport, Rhode Island
[August 18, 1790]
Gentlemen:

. . . The Citizens of the United States of America have a right to applaud themselves for having given to mankind examples of an enlarged and liberal policy: a policy worthy of imitation. All possess alike liberty of conscience and immunities [protections] of citizenship. It is now no more that toleration is spoken of, as if it was by the indulgence of one class of people, that another enjoyed the exercise of their inherent natural rights. For happily the Government of the United States, which gives to bigotry no sanction, to persecution no assistance, requires only that they who live under its protection should demean themselves as good citizens, in giving it on all occasions their effectual support. . . .

May the Children of the Stock of Abraham, who dwell in this land continue to merit and enjoy the good will of the other inhabitants. . . .

G. Washington
passage.citation: Source: President George Washington, Letter to the Hebrew Congregation of Newport, Rhode Island, August 18, 1790 (adapted)
passage._from: Sam 2026-11-02 09:01, typed from the NYSED crop and compared against the exam PDF's own text layer; Danny CLEARED 09:12, COUNT 14-0-0, source file md5 b4c6085aed34f4423757fd5b2c80da00

spans: All possess alike liberty of conscience
gives to bigotry no sanction, to persecution no assistance
items.why: Washington is writing to a Jewish congregation, and he says “All possess alike liberty of conscience”: everyone is equally free to hold their own beliefs. He adds that the government “gives to bigotry no sanction, to persecution no assistance.” A letter about equal freedom of belief is evidence of religious freedom in early United States history, choice 2.

items.era: The New Republic · The Bill of Rights (1791)
items.watch: The Articles of Confederation and the Great and Three-Fifths Compromises are all real founding-era deals — but none of them is a list of individual rights. Only one choice is.

For happily the Government of the United States, which gives to bigotry no sanction, to persecution no assistance, requires only that they who live under its protection should demean themselves as good citizens, in giving it on all occasions their effectual support. . . .

items.why: Washington's letter is about rights that belong to every person: he names “liberty of conscience” and says the government offers “persecution no assistance.” The Articles of Confederation and the two compromises are deals about how the government is built, not lists of individual rights. The Bill of Rights is the choice that guarantees rights like these.

items.watch: Choice (1) describes the OPPOSITE of what McCulloch actually held. If you remember ‘states vs. federal government’ but not which side won, you will pick the reverse of the real answer — McCulloch is a federal-supremacy case, not a states'-rights case.
items.stem: What was an important impact of the McCulloch v. Maryland (1819) decision?

options.1: It established the idea that states should have the power to overturn federal laws.
options.2: It determined that the creation of the National Bank was constitutional.
options.3: It stated that the bicameral legislature established by the Constitution was illegal.
options.4: It limited the power of Congress to add new states to the Union.

items.why: McCulloch v. Maryland decided whether the National Bank was constitutional. The Court said yes, and the necessary-and-proper clause is what makes it so, which is choice 2. Lock in the pair: McCulloch means the bank is constitutional, and in this case the federal government won.

items.watch: Republican government, popular sovereignty, and sectionalism are all real Unit 1-2 vocabulary — none of them is what happens when a STATE law loses to a FEDERAL one. Only one principle names that.
items.stem: The Supreme Court decision described in this excerpt is an example of which principle?

passage.text: . . . The result is a conviction that the States have no power, by taxation or otherwise, to retard [slow down], impede, burden, or in any manner control, the operations of the constitutional laws enacted by Congress to carry into execution the powers vested in the general government. This is, we think, the unavoidable consequence of that supremacy which the constitution has declared. We are unanimously of opinion, that the law passed by the legislature of Maryland, imposing a tax on the Bank of the United States, is unconstitutional and void. . . .
passage._from: Sam 2026-11-02 09:01, typed from the NYSED crop and compared against the exam PDF's own text layer; Danny CLEARED 09:12, COUNT 14-0-0, source file md5 b4c6085aed34f4423757fd5b2c80da00

spans: the States have no power, by taxation or otherwise
that supremacy which the constitution has declared
items.why: The Court says “the States have no power, by taxation or otherwise” to get in the way of Congress's laws, and it calls this the result of “that supremacy which the constitution has declared.” Maryland's tax on the Bank of the United States loses, because the Court says a law like that “is unconstitutional and void.” A state law losing to the Constitution is federal supremacy, choice 4.

items.watch: Military strength and industrial capacity are both real later arguments for American power — neither is Washington's 1796 argument, which rests on something the country simply HAS, not something it built.
items.stem: In this address, President George Washington states that the United States can stay out of foreign entanglements because of its

passage.text:
. . . The great rule of conduct for us, in regard to foreign Nations is in extending our commercial relations to have with them as little political connection as possible. So far as we have already formed engagements let them be fulfilled with perfect good faith. Here let us stop.

Europe has a set of primary interests, which to us have none, or a very remote relation. Hence she must be engaged in frequent controversies, the causes of which are essentially foreign to our concerns. Hence therefore it must be unwise in us to implicate ourselves, by artificial ties, in the ordinary vicissitudes [shifts] of her politics, or the ordinary combinations and collisions of her friendships, or enmities [hostilities].

Our detached and distant situation invites and enables us to pursue a different course. If we remain one People, under an efficient government, the period is not far off, when we may defy material injury from external annoyance; when we may take such an attitude as will cause the neutrality we may at any time resolve upon to be scrupulously [completely] respected; when belligerent nations, under the impossibility of making acquisitions upon us, will not lightly hazard the giving us provocation; when we may choose peace or War as our interest guided by justice shall counsel. . . .
passage.citation: Source: President George Washington, Farewell Address, 1796 (adapted)
passage._from: Sam 2026-11-02 09:01, typed from the NYSED crop and compared against the exam PDF's own text layer; Danny CLEARED 09:12, COUNT 14-0-0, source file md5 b4c6085aed34f4423757fd5b2c80da00

spans: invites and enables us to pursue a different course
items.why: Washington names the reason himself: “Our detached and distant situation” is how he describes where the United States sits, and he says it “invites and enables us to pursue a different course” from Europe's politics. A reason that comes from where the country is on the map is geographical location, choice 4.

items.watch: A judiciary did exist under the proposed Constitution, and the president was never popularly elected at the founding — two choices fail on fact alone, before you even weigh them against the passage.
items.stem: Based on this passage, why did Antifederalists oppose ratification of the Constitution?

options.1: The legislative branch had too much power.
options.2: A judicial branch did not exist.
options.3: The executive branch had no limits on its authority.
options.4: The president was elected by popular vote.

passage.text: . . . But to the question—without force what can restrain the Congress from making such laws as they please? What limits are there to their authority? I fear none at all. For surely it cannot be justly said that they have no power but what is expressly given to them, when by the very terms of their creation they are vested with the powers of making laws in all cases—necessary and proper; when from the nature of their power, they must necessarily be the judges what laws are necessary and proper. . . .
passage._from: live stimulus-11-2.json item 0824-mc08 - same NYSED crop unit02-0824-mc07.png, transcribed word for word

spans: what can restrain the Congress from making such laws as they please
What limits are there to their authority? I fear none at all.
items.why: He asks “what can restrain the Congress from making such laws as they please” and then pushes the point: “What limits are there to their authority? I fear none at all.” Congress is the legislative branch, so his complaint is that the legislative branch has too much power: choice 1.

items.era: Founding Principles · Virginia Declaration of Rights (1776)
items.watch: Separation of powers and federalism are both real principles — just not from the Declaration; they're structural ideas from the Constitution. This excerpt is about where government's power ORIGINATES, not how it's divided up.
items.stem: Which principle of the Declaration of Independence is reflected in this excerpt?

passage.text: . . . That all power is vested in, and consequently derived from, the people; that magistrates are their trustees and servants and at all times amenable to them. . . .
passage.citation: Source: Virginia Declaration of Rights, June 12, 1776
passage._from: Sam 2026-11-02 09:01, typed from the NYSED crop and compared against the exam PDF's own text layer; Danny CLEARED 09:12, COUNT 14-0-0, source file md5 b4c6085aed34f4423757fd5b2c80da00

spans: all power is vested in, and consequently derived from, the people
magistrates are their trustees and servants
items.why: The excerpt says “all power is vested in, and consequently derived from, the people.” It adds that “magistrates are their trustees and servants” — government officials work for the people. Power that comes from the people, with leaders answerable to them, is consent of the governed: choice 3.

items.watch: The Supreme Court, the cabinet, and state governors are all named somewhere else in the Constitution for other jobs — none of them is named here. Only one branch is given this specific power.
items.stem: The Constitution gives the power to determine presidential succession beyond the vice president to
items.why: The Constitution settles the first step itself: the vice president. For everyone after that, Article II, Section 1 hands the decision to one body, and that body is Congress. Congress is the branch that makes laws, so deciding the line of succession beyond the vice president is a lawmaking job, choice 3.

items.watch: Federalism and a two-party system are real later-era topics that do not belong to THIS author's 1787 argument — and ‘enough power to avoid tyranny’ is the Federalist position, the opposite of what an Antifederalist would claim.
items.stem: Which claim about the proposed United States Constitution is being made by the author of this passage?

options.1: The new Constitution gave the states enough power to avoid tyranny.
options.2: The elastic clause would give too much power to Congress.
options.3: The system of federalism is best for the new nation.
options.4: The two-party system would lead to rebellion in the future.

passage.text:
Centinel, no. 5

Fall 1787

. . . But the convention has superadded another power, by which the congress may stamp with the sanction of the constitution every possible law; it is contained in the following clause—“To make all laws which shall be necessary and proper for carrying into execution the foregoing powers, and all other powers vested by this constitution in the government of the United States, or in any department or officer thereof.” Whatever law congress may deem necessary and proper for carrying into execution any of the powers vested in them, may be enacted; and by virtue of this clause, they may controul [control] and abrogate [abolish] any and every of the laws of the state governments, on the allegation that they interfere with the execution of any of their powers, and yet these laws will “be made in pursuance [fulfillment] of the constitution,” and of course will “be the supreme law of the land, and the judges in every state shall be bound thereby, any thing in the constitution or laws of any state to the contrary notwithstanding.”
passage.citation: Source: Samuel Bryan, 1787; Herbert J. Storing, ed., The Complete Anti-Federalist, University of Chicago Press, 1981 (adapted)
passage._from: live stimulus-11-2.json item 0126-mc03 - same NYSED crop unit02-centinel-1787-doc1.png, transcribed word for word

spans: congress may stamp with the sanction of the constitution every possible law
To make all laws which shall be necessary and proper
items.why: Centinel says the convention added a power by which “congress may stamp with the sanction of the constitution every possible law” — and then he names the clause: “To make all laws which shall be necessary and proper.” A clause that lets Congress pass any law it deems necessary and proper is the elastic clause, and his complaint is that it gives Congress too much power: choice 2.
